study_identification_part.si4_title: Normative model detects abnormal functional connectivity in psychiatric disorders

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: This study proposes a normative model based on autoencoders to investigate if normative models based on functional connectivity can discriminate between different psychiatric disorders (SCZ, BD, ADHD) and address their heterogeneous nature.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Mann-Whitney U test for group comparisons of MSEs; Graph theory metrics (network degree); Subtraction of healthy control MSEf matrix from patient MSEf matrices to identify disorder-specific abnormalities.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: The normative model successfully identified functional connectivity patterns characteristic of SCZ, BD, and ADHD, showing that patients deviate significantly from healthy controls, though individual-level heterogeneity remains high.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: We found that the functional connectivity related to the basal ganglia network seems to play an important role in the neuropathology of BD and SCZ, whereas in ADHD, its role is less evident. Moreover, the abnormal connectivity between the basal ganglia network and the language network is more specific to BD. The connectivity between the higher visual network and the right executive control and the connectivity between the anterior salience network and the precuneus networks are the most relevant in SCZ and ADHD, respectively. Mann-Whitney test showed statistically significant differences in MSEs between healthy subjects and all patient groups (p < 0.05), but not between patient groups themselves (Table 3). Graph theory analysis showed patient groups had a greater number of connected FBNs (Figure 2A). Specific FBNs were identified as more abnormal for each disorder: ASN, HVN, LN, RECN, SN, VDMN, VN for ADHD; ASN, BGN, DDMN, HVN, LN, PSN for BD; ASN, BGN, HVN, LN, LECN, PSN, RECN, VDMN for SCZ (Figure 2B). Individual-level analysis revealed high heterogeneity within patient groups, indicating that group-level findings do not always resist individual-level analysis (Figure 6). The model generalized to an independent COBRE dataset for SCZ, showing similar patterns of abnormal FBNs, although statistical significance in distinguishing SCZ from HCs was lower (p=0.324) compared to the UCLA dataset.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study highlights the potential of DL-based normative models to bridge deep learning and precision medicine, enabling person-centered care by linking clinical symptoms to individual functional connectivity abnormalities and identifying subgroups within psychiatric disorders.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Limitations include: suboptimal scan duration/temporal resolution; non-specific dual regression template; lack of intranetwork connectivity exploration; small sample size; simple autoencoder without age/sex information; lack of control for treatment, disease severity, and course; and inherent instability of fMRI functional connectivity compared to structural MRI.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: The original paper is based on the master's dissertation of Oliveira-Saraiva. HAF is founder of NeuroPsyAI Ltd, a neurosciences service company using medical imaging. The study used 14 FBNs from Shirer et al. (48) as a template for dual regression. The study emphasizes that group-level differences do not resist individual-level analysis, supporting a precision-based medical approach for psychiatric disorders. The study used a threshold of 1 (corresponding to the 20% higher values of the merged difference vector) for binarizing the difference vectors into matrices for graph theory analysis. The study also performed an additional analysis with a larger H-Test-U set (78 healthy individuals) to robustly investigate FBNs characterizing patient groups.
